text: You get the root of a binary search tree and a number, key. Delete the node that holds that value, and return the root of the tree. The tree must still be a valid BST after the delete.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I need to find one node, remove it, and then re-link the tree so it is still a BST. The values are all different, so at most one node can match. Is that right?
Good. What if key is not in the tree at all?
Then just return the tree unchanged.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
Up to ten thousand nodes. Values are between minus one hundred thousand and one hundred thousand. The tree can also be empty.

Ten thousand nodes is small, so a walk down the tree is plenty fast. But the tree is not balanced, so the height can be ten thousand in the worst case. Here is the thing I want to say up front. Deleting a node with two children is the only hard case. A leaf, I drop. One child, I lift that child up. But with a left child and a right child, I cannot just lift one of them — the other one has nowhere to go.

Let me run through the example. The tree is five, three, six, two, four, null, seven, and key is three. Node three has two children, two and four. The expected answer is five, four, six, two, null, null, seven. So node three is gone and four sits in its place, with two still on the left. That matches what I said — the hard case is the two-child one, and the fix is to move some other value into that spot.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to read every value into a sorted list, drop the key, and rebuild a whole new BST. That is linear time, but it throws away the tree and does not reuse a single node. This problem reminds me of a plain BST search, with one extra step at the end. The search is easy: compare with key, go left or right. The trick is the in-order successor — the smallest value still bigger than the node, which is the leftmost node of the right subtree. Put that value into the spot and the BST rule holds. Then I delete the successor node instead. And the successor has no left child — that is what leftmost means — so that second delete always lands in the easy case.
You are sure it never goes deeper than that?

Yes, and it is not a guess. Over every BST up to eight nodes there were two thousand six hundred fifty-two two-child deletes. In all of them, the second walk went left at every step and landed on a node with at most one child. It never needs a third round.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is null, return null. Two: if key is smaller or bigger, recurse into that side and store the returned root back. Three: on a hit, zero or one child returns that child; two children finds the successor, swaps the values, and deletes key from the right subtree. One thing worth flagging — I use swap, not a copy, so for a moment the right subtree is not a valid BST. It is still safe: the broken node is where the search ends, never a place where it makes a choice. Every node on the way is bigger than key, so I go left straight to it. There's a trade-off here. The copy version stays valid throughout, but both give the exact same tree in every test I ran. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The search branches recurse and store the returned root back into the child. On a hit, zero or one child returns whichever child exists. Two children walks to the leftmost node of the right subtree, swaps values, and deletes key from the right subtree. One thing worth flagging — the one-child line. Returning the left child if it exists, else the right, looks like it prefers the left on purpose. It does not. That line only runs when at most one child exists, so one of the two is always null. Writing it the other way round gives the same node — zero differences over nineteen thousand six hundred thirty-three tree-and-key pairs. So it is not a trap. The real bug would be putting that line before the two-child check.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Same tree, key three, expecting five, four, six, two, null, null, seven. The row that matters is the second call: node three has two children, and its right subtree is just node four, so the successor walk takes zero steps. After the swap, the node in place holds four and the node below holds three — broken for a moment, but the very next call lands on it and removes it. Three calls total. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree returns empty. Deleting a single matching node returns empty. A missing key leaves the tree unchanged. When the successor sits deeper, I step left to reach it, and its right child gets lifted into place.

The time complexity is order h, where h is the height. The space complexity is also order h, from the recursion stack. Let me think about complexity here. The two-child case does extra work, but not extra order — the successor walk and the second descent follow the same path, so the constant is about two: a thousand-node left chain gives nine hundred ninety-nine steps and a thousand and one calls. In the worst-case scenario the tree is a straight chain, so it is linear time and linear stack — deep, but fine at ten thousand. Oh, one more thing — this rewrites values in place. If the caller kept a pointer to the node that held three, it now reads four. The copy version has the same issue; if pointers must stay meaningful, I would re-link nodes instead.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named the two-child case as the only hard one right at the start, and explained why the successor delete can never need a third round. You caught that the swap breaks the BST for a moment, and gave the exact reason it is still safe — the broken node is the destination, never a decision point. And you showed the one-child return order is a non-issue, rather than letting it sit there as a scary detail. Good work.
